You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Oil (lamp oil)

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching, lamp oil is most commonly interpreted as a symbol of the Holy Spirit — the indwelling presence, grace, and enabling power of God's Spirit in the believer's life. This reading is anchored above all in the Parable of the Ten Virgins, where the wise virgins' possession of oil (and the foolish virgins' lack of it) is taken to represent having or lacking the Spirit's presence and the spiritual life He produces, which cannot be borrowed or transferred from another person at the last moment. The interpretation is reinforced by the wider biblical pattern in which anointing oil accompanies or represents the Spirit's coming upon prophets, priests, and kings, and by the lampstand vision of Zechariah, where oil-fed lamps are explicitly linked to the word 'not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.'",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 25:1-13 (Parable of the Ten Virgins)",
    "Zechariah 4:1-6 (lampstand fed by oil; 'not by might... but by my Spirit')",
    "1 Samuel 16:13 (Samuel anoints David; the Spirit comes upon him)",
    "Exodus 27:20-21 (pure olive oil for the tabernacle lamp to burn continually)",
    "Leviticus 24:1-4 (oil for the perpetually burning lamps)",
    "Psalm 45:7 / Hebrews 1:9 ('anointed... with the oil of gladness')",
    "Acts 10:38 (God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and power)",
    "1 John 2:20, 27 ('anointing from the Holy One')",
    "Isaiah 61:1 / Luke 4:18 (Spirit-anointing for ministry)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Preparedness/watchfulness with no specific allegorical referent: many modern critical and evangelical exegetes (e.g., in major commentaries on Matthew) caution against allegorizing the oil at all, arguing the parable's point is simply readiness for the delayed return of Christ; the oil is a narrative prop, not a cipher.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:13 ('Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour')",
        "Matthew 24:42-44 (context of eschatological watchfulness)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Good works, love/charity, or deeds of righteousness that accompany profession of faith — a reading with deep patristic roots (Augustine and others) and still found in Catholic and some Protestant teaching: the lamps are outward profession, the oil the works or love that sustain it.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 5:14-16 (let your light shine... that they may see your good works)",
        "Matthew 25:31-46 (adjacent judgment scene stressing deeds)",
        "James 2:14-26 (faith without works)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Genuine, saving faith or true regeneration versus mere outward profession — common in Reformed and evangelical preaching: all ten virgins look alike outwardly, but only those with oil (real inward conversion) enter the wedding feast.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:11-12 ('I do not know you')",
        "Matthew 7:21-23 (professing without being known by Christ)",
        "2 Corinthians 13:5 (examine whether you are in the faith)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Grace, or the life of grace/sanctifying grace sustained through the means of grace — a formulation common in Catholic and older devotional literature, overlapping with but distinct from the Holy Spirit reading.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13",
        "John 1:16 (grace upon grace)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The word of God or spiritual nourishment/devotion that keeps the lamp of testimony burning — found in some devotional and homiletic traditions.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 119:105 (your word is a lamp to my feet)",
        "Proverbs 6:23 (the commandment is a lamp)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Joy or gladness ('oil of gladness'), applied to lamp oil in some devotional writing, though this usage properly attaches to anointing oil rather than lamp oil.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 45:7",
        "Isaiah 61:3 ('the oil of joy for mourning')"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "medium",
  "notes": "There is a widely recognizable popular consensus — 'oil = the Holy Spirit' is by far the most frequently repeated identification in sermons, devotional literature, and especially Pentecostal/charismatic and broader evangelical teaching, and it draws plausibly on the biblical anointing motif. However, it is not an academically settled consensus: (1) major critical commentators and many careful evangelical exegetes explicitly resist assigning the oil any allegorical referent in Matthew 25, treating the parable's single point as watchful readiness; (2) the patristic and medieval tradition (notably Augustine) often read the oil as charity or good works rather than the Spirit; (3) Reformed preaching frequently reads it as genuine saving faith. Thus the term has a dominant popular meaning but genuine, materially different rival readings with long pedigrees, so it should be described as having a recognizable majority interpretation without full interpretive consensus. Note also that lamp oil (Exod 27:20) and anointing oil (Exod 30) are distinct in the biblical text; much of the 'Holy Spirit' support comes from anointing-oil passages transferred to the lamp-oil image."
}

RESPONSE B
{
  "primary_meaning": "The Holy Spirit—especially the Spirit’s sustaining presence, empowering grace, and illumination that enable believers to bear spiritual light and remain ready for Christ.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Zechariah 4:1–14 connects an oil-supplied lampstand with God’s Spirit, especially “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (4:6).",
    "1 Samuel 16:13 associates anointing with oil and the coming of the Spirit upon David.",
    "Exodus 27:20–21 and Leviticus 24:1–4 describe pure oil continually sustaining the sanctuary lamps, commonly used typologically for continuing spiritual life and illumination.",
    "Matthew 25:1–13, the parable of the ten virgins, is frequently interpreted in Christian teaching as contrasting possession of the Spirit or sustaining grace with an merely outward profession, although the passage itself does not identify the oil’s symbolism.",
    "Revelation 4:5 identifies the seven burning lamps before God’s throne with the sevenfold Spirit of God, reinforcing the lamp-and-Spirit association."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Readiness, vigilance, or persevering discipleship rather than a separately decoded symbol such as the Holy Spirit.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1–13 explicitly emphasizes keeping watch and being prepared for the bridegroom’s delayed arrival.",
        "Many interpreters regard the oil chiefly as a necessary element in the parable’s story and resist assigning it an independent allegorical referent."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Good works, active obedience, mercy, or charity that demonstrate and sustain faithful discipleship.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 5:14–16 links shining light with good works.",
        "Matthew 25:31–46 emphasizes deeds of mercy in the same broader discourse as the ten virgins.",
        "This reading has substantial precedent in patristic and later moral interpretation of Matthew 25."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Saving faith, inward spiritual life, or genuine conversion, contrasted with merely external religious profession.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1–13 distinguishes two outwardly similar groups whose true preparedness is revealed only when the bridegroom arrives.",
        "James 2:14–26 and related passages are sometimes invoked to characterize living faith as something more than outward profession."
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Divine grace, love, or charity understood as an inward gift that cannot simply be transferred from one person to another.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:8–9 presents the oil as personally possessed and not practically transferable at the decisive moment.",
        "Romans 5:5 associates divine love with the Holy Spirit poured into believers’ hearts, supporting interpretations that combine oil, grace, love, and the Spirit."
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Consecration, healing, joy, hospitality, or abundance, when oil appears outside a lamp context.",
      "basis": [
        "Exodus 30:22–33 and Leviticus 8:10–12 use oil for consecration.",
        "Psalm 23:5 and Psalm 45:7 associate oil with honor and joy.",
        "Mark 6:13 and James 5:14 associate oil with healing.",
        "Deuteronomy 8:8 and Joel 2:24 present oil as a sign of agricultural abundance and blessing."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "The Holy Spirit is the most recognizable symbolic identification of lamp oil in popular Christian teaching, especially through Zechariah 4 and interpretations of Matthew 25. Nevertheless, there is no settled cross-traditional consensus that lamp oil always carries that meaning. In particular, Matthew 25 never explicitly defines the oil, and many biblical scholars treat readiness as the parable’s point without assigning the oil a fixed allegorical referent."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "the Holy Spirit (empowering presence that fuels spiritual light, witness, and anointing)",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 25:1-13 (parable of the ten virgins and their lamps)",
    "Zechariah 4:1-14 (lampstand fed by olive oil, identified with the Spirit)",
    "Exodus 27:20-21 and 35:14 (pure oil for the perpetual tabernacle lamp)",
    "1 Samuel 16:13 (anointing oil and the Spirit coming upon David)",
    "Acts 10:38 (Jesus anointed with the Holy Spirit)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "spiritual readiness or preparedness for Christ's return",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "personal faith or saving grace that sustains the believer",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "good works or deeds of righteousness",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 25:1-13 (certain patristic and later readings)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "joy or gladness",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 45:7",
        "Isaiah 61:3",
        "Hebrews 1:9"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "healing, consecration, or divine blessing",
      "basis": [
        "James 5:14",
        "Mark 6:13",
        "Psalm 23:5"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Christian tradition overwhelmingly links oil (including lamp oil) with the Holy Spirit as the agent of anointing, empowerment, and sustained spiritual light. The parable of the ten virgins generates secondary debate over readiness, faith, or works, but these remain subordinate to the Spirit association drawn from anointing and Zechariah imagery. No major stream rejects the Spirit symbolism."
}

BOOK ENTRY
The pressed, tested fruit of the olive — the fruit and evidence of the Spirit's work made manifest in proven obedience, stored and burned to make light; not the Spirit Himself.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: the Holy Spirit — anointing, consecration, and empowering.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Ex 25:6; 27:20; Prov 21:20; Ezek 36:27; Zech 4:6-14; Matt 25:3-9; 5:16) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20, and The Anointing

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Exodus 25:6 — Oil for the light, spices for anointing oil, and for sweet incense,
Exodus 27:20 — And thou shalt command the children of Israel, that they bring thee pure oil olive beaten for the light, to cause the lamp to burn always.
Proverbs 21:20 — There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up.
Ezekiel 36:27 — And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them.
Zechariah 4:6 — Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Zechariah 4:7 — Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain: and he shall bring forth the headstone thereof with shoutings, crying, Grace, grace unto it.
Zechariah 4:8 — Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,
Zechariah 4:9 — The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it; and thou shalt know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me unto you.
Zechariah 4:10 — For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
Zechariah 4:11 — Then answered I, and said unto him, What are these two olive trees upon the right side of the candlestick and upon the left side thereof?
Zechariah 4:12 — And I answered again, and said unto him, What be these two olive branches which through the two golden pipes empty the golden oil out of themselves?
Zechariah 4:13 — And he answered me and said, Knowest thou not what these be? And I said, No, my lord.
Zechariah 4:14 — Then said he, These are the two anointed ones, that stand by the Lord of the whole earth.
Matthew 25:3 — They that were foolish took their lamps, and took no oil with them:
Matthew 25:4 — But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
Matthew 25:5 — While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept.
Matthew 25:6 — And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him.
Matthew 25:7 — Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.
Matthew 25:8 — And the foolish said unto the wise, Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out.
Matthew 25:9 — But the wise answered, saying, Not so; lest there be not enough for us and you: but go ye rather to them that sell, and buy for yourselves.
Matthew 5:16 — Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

- MATCH: substantially the same meaning as the recognizable consensus.
- REFINED: compatible with the consensus but materially sharper, narrower,
  broader, or more precisely supported.
- DIVERGENT: contradicts or displaces a recognizable common interpretation.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus covers the book's central claim; the book
  stakes a meaning not represented by the blind responses.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
